name: NIST on AI Risk Management and Standards for Industry
title: NIST on AI Risk Management and Standards for Industry
answer: NIST publishes the AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0), a voluntary, non-sector-specific resource for organizations designing, developing, deploying or using AI, plus a Roadmap of follow-on activities and a programme of AI standards work. For manufacturers the most useful element is the framework's cross-sectoral Profiles, which let a sector document how it applies the framework in practice, alongside NIST's stated priority of aligning the framework with international standards such as ISO/IEC 42001.

sections.body: The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), part of the US Department of Commerce, publishes these pages. They cover the AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0), released on January 26, 2023, its companion Roadmap, the AI Standards Zero Drafts project, and NIST's role as federal AI standards coordinator. The material is guidance rather than regulation: the framework is described as voluntary, rights-preserving, non-sector specific and use-case agnostic. NIST states that the National Artificial Intelligence Initiative Act of 2020 directed the framework's goal of helping organizations manage AI risks and promote trustworthy and responsible development and use.
sections.heading: What this source is

sections.body: The AI RMF is intended to help organizations incorporate trustworthiness considerations into the design, development, use and evaluation of AI products, services and systems. It was developed through a consensus-driven, open and collaborative process involving a Request for Information, several public draft versions and multiple workshops. The Roadmap sets out activities that NIST or other organizations may carry out to advance the framework, including tools, benchmarks, testbeds and standardized methodologies for evaluating AI risks and system trustworthiness, including from a socio-technical lens. Profiles are the primary method for organizations to share real-life examples of putting the framework into practice, and may be sector-specific, cross-sectoral, temporal or topical. NIST encourages organizations and individuals to produce profiles jointly or independently, and intends to develop case studies of framework use. The framework is being revised as part of the White House AI Action Plan, and on April 7, 2026 NIST released a concept note for an AI RMF Profile on Trustworthy AI in Critical Infrastructure. NIST also runs an AI Standards Zero Drafts project, which produces preliminary, stakeholder-driven drafts for submission into the private sector-led voluntary consensus standards process.
sections.heading: What it says

sections.body: The AI RMF 1.0 was released on January 26, 2023. A concept note for an AI RMF Profile on Trustworthy AI in Critical Infrastructure was released on April 7, 2026. An initial public draft of Guidance and Templates for Public-Facing AI Documentation: An AI Standards Zero Draft was released on July 29, 2026, with input considered until September 16, 2026. A Plan for Global Engagement on AI Standards (NIST AI 100-5e2025) was released on July 26, 2024, following a draft of April 29, 2024. The Roadmap cites alignment with ISO/IEC 5338, 38507, 22989, 24028, DIS 42001 and NP 42005, and the first two AI RMF crosswalks cover ISO/IEC FDIS 23894 and the OECD Recommendation on AI, the Proposed EU AI Act and other documents.
sections.heading: Figures and claims worth noting

sections.body: A manufacturer following AI needs a common vocabulary for risk and trustworthiness, and this is where the US federal version of it is written. The framework's non-sector-specific design means it can be applied to production use cases without a manufacturing-specific rewrite, while the Profiles mechanism gives a route for a sector to publish how it actually applies the framework. The stated priority of aligning the framework with international standards, and the crosswalks to ISO/IEC documents, matter to firms whose equipment and software supply chains cross borders. The Roadmap's emphasis on testbeds, benchmarks and evaluation methodologies is directly relevant to anyone who has to test a model before it touches a line.
sections.heading: What it means for AI in Manufacturing

sections.body: The framework is voluntary and non-sector specific, so it prescribes no manufacturing requirements, no thresholds and no compliance obligations. The pages are largely programme and process descriptions: they explain what NIST intends to do and how organizations may participate, not what a plant should deploy. Several items are drafts or concept notes open for comment, and NIST states that its involvement in Roadmap activities will depend in part on resources available. The material is also dated by its publication sequence, with revisions to AI RMF 1.0 still in progress.
